name: Priya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding machines at Brightpak, a plant on the edge of town that makes plastic food tubs and lids. Moulding means melting plastic pellets and squirting them into a steel mould, then the part pops out. I start at six, check the hopper's full, watch the first parts for flash, which is the thin extra plastic around the edge, and box what comes off the conveyor. I've been there just over a year, so I still call the setter, Kwame, when a mould sticks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you live with, and how are things at home money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the part that wears me out is the noise and standing on concrete for eight hours. The part I like is when a whole run comes out clean and I've caught a problem before it turned into two thousand bad lids. I'm in the union, and I go to the meetings in the canteen even though half of it is people complaining about the vending machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the canteen: told you so. Every year the bosses promise some new system will change everything, and we still end up scraping lids off the floor by hand. Online I'd probably share a meme about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Brightpak lost a big supermarket contract last spring, and we went down to four-day weeks for two months. If AI is a flop, the lost supermarket contract and the four-day weeks are still sitting there. Nothing changing isn't the same as everything being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep learning the machines properly, so I'm not the weakest one if they cut a shift. I'd keep putting about a hundred a month into savings, because we've got roughly three months put by. And I'd push at the union meeting to get short-time pay written down properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit tired. It's the same low hum of worry I already carry every time the order board looks thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev, my partner, that it's one less thing on the pile but the pile's still there. He works nights at a parcel depot, so between us we're always one bad month from dipping into savings. We'd still skip the holiday and keep the money where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame, the setter, actually. He's the only one who really knows the old moulds, and if he left, the line would fall apart. Management keeps saying they'll train someone else, and they never do.

say: I'd tell the canteen it's **the usual hype** and the bosses oversold it again.
I'd share a joke online and not make a big deal of it.
think: Privately, the **lost contract** and four-day weeks still worry me more than any AI.
Nothing changing still leaves Brightpak **one bad order** away from cutting shifts.
do: Keep **learning the machines** properly so I'm not first to go if shifts are cut.
Keep saving about **a hundred a month** on top of three months put by.
Push the union to write **short-time pay** rules down properly.
feel: Flat and tired, with a **low hum of worry** about the order board.
S0.quote: If AI is a flop, the lost supermarket contract and the four-day weeks are still sitting there. Nothing changing isn't the same as everything being fine.
fieldNote: Her worry starts with **the firm's orders**, not with technology at all.
She leans on **the union** as her first tool, which fits her politics.
Kwame (the setter) is the person she sees as **holding the line together**.

steps.text: Ask Kwame to teach her the sticky moulds on quiet shifts
Save about a hundred a month into the joint account
Raise short-time pay rules at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the office will feel this before we do, which is true. Scheduling, purchasing, quality reports, that's all screen stuff. I'd also say we need the union at the table now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the office getting smaller is the start, not the end. If the planning goes to software, the next thing they'll look at is the cost per tub, and that's us. Brightpak already has one robot arm that stacks lids on line four, and it doesn't take tea breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be trained on the robot arm on line four, because the people who look after it seem safer. I'd try one of those AI chat tools to understand the machine manuals, which I've only done a couple of times. I'd also raise retraining money at the union, so the firm pays for courses and not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. There's time in this one, and I keep thinking about how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office feels it first. Do you know anyone in the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's been told to try new planning software already. My friend Lena does the production schedule, and she jokes that she's training her own replacement. I laughed, then went home and looked at robot arm jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership goes first, then eating out on Fridays. Dev and I would keep the rent and the car paid before anything. The car matters because the bus doesn't reach the plant before six.

say: I'd say **the office** feels this first, with planning and purchasing going to software.
I'd say the union needs a **seat at the table** now, not later.
think: Privately, once planning is software, **cost per tub** becomes the next target, and that's us.
The **robot arm** on line four already does a person's job without breaks.
do: Ask for **robot arm** training on line four within six months.
Use an **AI chat tool** to read machine manuals, which I've barely tried.
Push the union for **firm-paid retraining**, not courses we pay for.
feel: **Anxious but not frozen**, because there is still time to act.
S1.quote: My friend Lena does the production schedule, and she jokes that she's training her own replacement. I laughed, then went home and looked at robot arm jobs.
fieldNote: She reads Steady Disruption as **office first, line second**, and plans for the second wave.
Her steady streak shows: she'll try AI tools, but **only for manuals**.
Money is tight enough that she has already **ranked her cuts**: gym, then Friday meals.

steps.text: Ask the shift manager for training on the line four robot arm
Use an AI chat tool to decode the moulding machine manuals
Push the union to win firm-paid retraining courses
Drop the gym membership if her hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is exactly why we need a government that steps in, with a wage guarantee or something like it. I'd post that online and I'd mean it. I'd also say the bosses will grab the savings and leave us with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got three years and then the robots come for the hands-on part. The thinking stuff, the ordering and scheduling, goes in 2028, and the plant will be quieter and meaner straight away. By 2031 a robot will box tubs better than me, and I'm still the junior one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop the holiday fund and put everything into savings, trying to get from three to six months. In the first year I'd sign up for an electrical maintenance course at the college at night, because someone has to fix the robots. And I'd go to every union meeting and every protest about a wage guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. My stomach drops when I picture the line with no people on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years before the robots come is the only thing that makes this bearable. Three years is long enough to get a maintenance certificate if I start straight away. If the robots came at the same time as the AI, I'd have nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev that the parcel depot is going the same way, so we can't count on his job to carry mine. We'd have to sit down with the bank app and work out how long we last. I think it's about five months if we're careful.

say: I'd say government must step in with **a wage guarantee** for workers like us.
I'd say the bosses will **keep the savings** and leave workers with nothing.
think: Privately, I think I get **three years** before robots take the hands-on part.
As the **junior operator**, I'd be among the first boxed out by 2031.
do: Stop the holiday fund and push savings from **three to six months**.
Start a **night course** in electrical maintenance at the college in the first year.
Join every **union meeting and protest** about a wage guarantee.
feel: **Scared**, with a sinking feeling picturing the line with no people.
S2.quote: The three years before the robots come is the only thing that makes this bearable. Three years is long enough to get a maintenance certificate if I start straight away.
fieldNote: She splits the threat clearly: **thinking work in 2028**, her hands-on job by 2031.
Both household jobs are exposed, so she can't lean on **Dev's income** (her partner).
Her plan is concrete but depends on **finishing a course**, which worries her.

steps.text: Move the holiday fund into savings to reach six months
Enrol in a night course in electrical maintenance at the college
Go to union meetings and protests for a wage guarantee
Vote for a party promising income support for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse this time. Companies and the government have five years to set up retraining and support. I'd share that online and tag our local MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years plus three more for robots is a real window. That's 2034 for the line, so I'd be about thirty-five. It's enough time to get qualified if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the electrical course part-time and keep working full shifts. I'd keep saving a hundred a month and maybe a bit more once Dev gets his pay rise. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd apply for maintenance jobs at bigger plants that are already using robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but a bit hopeful. It feels like a hill I could actually climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could stop you finishing the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly, if the course fees go up or my hours get cut. I quit a forklift course two years ago because night classes after a six o'clock start are brutal. I can't quit the electrical course this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, if they pocket the gains and don't train anyone. And the government, if it sits on its hands for five years and then acts surprised.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** this time, with five years of warning.
I'd tag **our local MP** online and ask about retraining plans.
think: Privately, robots on the line by **2034** leaves me a real window.
Being about **thirty-five** then feels young enough to change trades.
do: Start the **electrical course** part-time this year while working full shifts.
Keep saving **a hundred a month**, more once Dev's pay rises.
Apply for **maintenance jobs** at bigger, robot-heavy plants after AGI arrives.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, like a hill I could actually climb.
S3.quote: I quit a forklift course two years ago because night classes after a six o'clock start are brutal. I can't quit the electrical course this time.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her fear into **a step-by-step plan**.
She is honest about her **track record** of quitting a course.
Her job still goes by 2034, so her **income risk** stays real despite the hope.

steps.text: Start the part-time electrical maintenance course this year
Keep saving a hundred a month and raise it after Dev's pay rise
Apply for maintenance roles at robot-heavy plants nearby
Write to the local MP asking about retraining funding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if people actually use it. At work I'd tell the younger ones not to wait. Online I'd probably say less, because ten years sounds far away to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long for me but short for the firm. Brightpak might not last ten years anyway with the contracts we're losing. Robots on the line by 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine, probably in a different job already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical course next September, not this week, and space it out so I don't burn out. I'd save steadily and maybe talk to Dev about buying a small flat in five years. I'd keep going to the union, but I wouldn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but still a knot. My job's still going in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dev think about buying a flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev wants it more than me. I keep saying we shouldn't sign a mortgage when both our jobs could be robots by 2039. We'd probably wait until I've got the maintenance certificate in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long warning make it easier to put things off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ten years is long enough for me to tell myself I'll start the course next year, every single year. That's what scares me about the slow one.

say: I'd say ten years is enough time **if people use it**.
I'd tell younger workers on the line **not to wait**.
think: Privately, Brightpak might not last **ten years** anyway with lost contracts.
Robots on the line by **2039** mean I'll likely need another job.
do: Start the **electrical course** next September and pace it to avoid burnout.
Save steadily and **delay the flat** until the certificate is in hand.
Keep going to **union meetings** without panicking.
feel: Calmer than the faster pictures, but **still a knot** about the job.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to tell myself I'll start the course next year, every single year. That's what scares me about the slow one.
fieldNote: She spots her own risk of **putting things off** when the deadline is far.
The firm's **weak order book** stays her nearer worry.
A planned flat purchase becomes a family decision **tied to retraining**.

steps.text: Enrol in the electrical maintenance course next September
Save steadily from each payslip into the joint account
Hold off buying a flat with Dev until she's certified
Keep attending union meetings at the plant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because Dev and I would both be exposed and I'm the junior on the line. What would help is a wage guarantee while people retrain, and the firm paying for courses instead of making us do it on our own time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the robot arm. Nobody asked us before the robot arm came in on line four, and that's the part that gets me. Nobody asks the people on the floor.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked us before the robot arm came in on line four, and that's the part that gets me. Nobody asks the people on the floor.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old moulding operator**, a year into the job and still learning the machines.
She lives with **Dev (her partner)**, a night worker at a parcel depot, on about three months of savings.
Her first defence is **the union**, and she wants government to guarantee wages during change.
She plans to **retrain in electrical maintenance**, but knows she quit a course before.
Her mood tracks the **time before robots**: alarmed at 2028, anxious but hopeful with more warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because both household jobs would be exposed at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage guarantee** while people retrain, and **firm-paid courses** in work time.
